extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examiners on admitting, evaluating, and commenting on affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.131 and 1.132 and for assessing evidence of nonobviousness (secondary considerations). Emphasizes timeliness, sufficiency, probative value, nexus, and weighing of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority rights for inventors domiciled abroad while serving for home country
rubrics_metrics.description: If an invention was made by a person while domiciled in the United States (or a NAFTA country or WTO member country) and serving in another country in connection with operations by or on behalf of that country, that person is entitled to the same rights of priority in the United States as if the invention had been made in that country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes specific domiciliary categories (U.S., NAFTA, WTO member). This rule ensures entitlement to priority when inventor was serving abroad in connection with operations by or on behalf of their domiciliary country.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of foreign information when unavailable in U.S.
rubrics_metrics.description: When information in a NAFTA or WTO member country relevant to proving/disproving a date of invention has not been made available for use in PTO proceedings or in courts to the same extent as in the U.S., appropriate inferences or other actions must be taken in favor of the party that requested the information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Director, court, or other authority should draw inferences or take other statutorily, regulatory or rule-permitted actions in favor of the requester when foreign information cannot be made available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit/declaration allegation of location of acts (37 CFR 1.131)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 37 CFR 1.131 affidavit or declaration must allege that the acts relied upon to establish the date prior to the reference or activity were carried out in the United States or in a NAFTA or WTO member country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 35 U.S.C. 104 for statutory basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective dates for establishing completion in NAFTA/WTO countries
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 37 CFR 1.131 an applicant can establish a date of completion in a NAFTA country on or after December 8, 1993, and in a WTO member country (other than a NAFTA country) on or after January 1, 1996; dates of completion may not be established under 37 CFR 1.131 before those dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts occurring prior to those effective dates may be relied upon to show completion, but a date of completion cannot be established under 1.131 before those statutory effective dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhibit compliance with 37 CFR 1.91
rubrics_metrics.description: Exhibits filed as part of an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 must comply with 37 CFR 1.91 to be entered into an application file.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exhibits that do not comply may be disposed of or returned to applicant at the Office's discretion. See also MPEP § 608.03(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary examiner decision on sufficiency (37 CFR 1.131)
rubrics_metrics.description: The question of sufficiency of affidavits or declarations under 37 CFR 1.131 should be reviewed and decided by a primary examiner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal sufficiency/propriety issues are by petition (Technology Center Directors); review on merits is by appeal to the Board of Patent Appeals and Interferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seasonable presentation / timeliness rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.131 must be timely presented to be admitted. They are timely if submitted (A) prior to a final rejection, (B) before appeal in an application without a final rejection, or (C) after final rejection if submitted (1) with a first reply after final rejection to overcome a new ground/requirement, (2) with a satisfactory showing under 37 CFR 1.116(b) or 1.195, or (3) under 37 CFR 1.129(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All admitted affidavits/declarations are acknowledged and commented upon by the examiner in the next action. Refusal to enter as untimely is reviewed by petition, not by appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgement and commentary requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: All entered affidavits, declarations, and other evidence traversing rejections must be acknowledged and commented upon by the examiner in the next succeeding action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The extent of commentary depends on the examiner's action; if evidence overcomes the prima facie case, comments should follow guidelines for reasons for allowance. If insufficient, the examiner must specifically explain why.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 CFR 1.132 evidence formality requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: When any claim is rejected or objected to, any evidence submitted to traverse the rejection/objection on a basis not otherwise provided for must be by way of an oath or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule is the general policy for receiving affidavit evidence traversing rejections or objections that do not fall under other specific rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary examiner responsibility for 1.132 affidavits
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary examiner is responsible to personally review and decide whether affidavits/declarations submitted under 37 CFR 1.132 are responsive to the rejection and present sufficient facts to overcome the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must ensure the affidavit/declaration is directed to the rejection and contains sufficient factual evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of form paragraphs 7.65/7.66 for office actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph 7.65 (effective to withdraw rejection) and 7.66 (insufficient) and the set 7.66.01–7.66.05 form paragraphs should be used as appropriate to comment on 37 CFR 1.132 affidavits/declarations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each form paragraph contains bracketed fields for insertion (e.g., filing date, affected claims, statutory grounds). When using 7.66, follow with detailed reasons for insufficiency (untimely, fails to set forth facts, not commensurate in scope, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph 7.65 — sufficient to overcome rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Template wording to state that the affidavit/declaration filed on [date] is sufficient to overcome the rejection of claim(s) [x] based upon [statutory grounds/reference].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert appropriate bracketed items; examiner note fields for internal use. Use when the affidavit/declaration adequately rebuts the rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph 7.66 — affidavit/declaration insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Template wording to state that the affidavit/declaration filed on [date] is insufficient to overcome the rejection of claim(s) [x] based upon [statutory grounds/reference] as set forth in the last Office action because: [reasons].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After this paragraph, set forth reasons for insufficiency (e.g., untimely, fails to set forth facts, not commensurate in scope). Include detailed explanation and use specific subparagraphs 7.66.01–7.66.05 as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficiency reason — affiant has never seen invention
rubrics_metrics.description: If an affidavit includes statements affirming the affiant has never seen the claimed subject matter before, such statements are not relevant to nonobviousness and provide no objective evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precede this subparagraph with 7.66 and provide full explanation if appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficiency reason — invention works as intended
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements that merely affirm the claimed subject matter functions as intended are not relevant to nonobviousness and provide no objective evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such conclusory functional statements lack probative value for nonobviousness and require additional factual support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficiency reason — refers only to invention, not claims
rubrics_metrics.description: If the affidavit/declaration refers only to the system described in the application and not to the individual claims, it does not show that objective evidence of nonobviousness is commensurate in scope with the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits must address the claimed limitations, not just a general embodiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficiency reason — no evidence of long-felt need
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertions that the claimed subject matter solved a long-standing problem are insufficient without showing that others of ordinary skill were working on the problem, for how long, and that knowledge of the prior art would not have enabled solving it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide evidence that others were working and still unable to solve the problem despite knowledge of prior art; mere assertion is inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficiency reason — ultimate conclusion (7.66.05)
rubrics_metrics.description: When, after considering all evidence, the totality of rebuttal evidence fails to outweigh evidence of obviousness, state that conclusion as the final insufficiency paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present this paragraph as a conclusion and precede it with form paragraph 7.66 and a full factual explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness as a threshold for consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence traversing rejections must be timely or seasonably filed to be entered and entitled to consideration; timeliness follows the seasonable presentation rules (prior to final, before appeal, or after final under specified conditions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Rothermel and apply 1.131/1.132 timing rules; untimely submissions may be refused entry and such refusals are reviewed by petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration obligation — examiner must consider entered evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever entered, evidence traversing rejections must be considered by the examiner. The examiner must acknowledge and comment in the next action, explaining sufficiency or insufficiency specifically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid vague statements like 'declaration lacks technical validity' without explaining why. If evidence overcomes prima facie, comments should align with reasons-for-allowance guidance (MPEP § 1302.14).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective (secondary) evidence must be considered
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits/declarations containing evidence of criticality, unexpected results, commercial success, long-felt need, failure of others, skepticism of experts, etc., must be considered in determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court precedent (Stratoflex, Graham, etc.) requires consideration of secondary considerations when present; such evidence may shed light on circumstances of the invention's origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative data in specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners must consider comparative data in the specification intended to illustrate the claimed invention when reaching a conclusion regarding obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Margolis; lack of comparative data can weaken assertions of unexpected results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of objective evidence does not prove obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Absence of objective evidence of nonobviousness does not weigh in favor of obviousness, but where a prima facie case is established, failure to rebut with evidence can be dispositive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Miles Labs; if prima facie case exists, applicant's failure to provide rebuttal evidence may determine outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nexus requirement for secondary evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Any secondary evidence (commercial success, etc.) must be related to the claimed invention (a factual and legal 'nexus') to be probative of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must determine nexus between objective evidence and claimed invention; rely on case law (Ashland Oil, Demaco) to assess connection and probative value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probative value requires factual support (objective evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence (unexpected results, commercial success, long-felt need, derivation allegations, invention before date of reference, inoperability of prior art) should be supported by appropriate affidavits/declarations to be of probative value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples (De Blauwe, Lindner, George) emphasize need for factual experimental data or documentary support rather than bare assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attorney arguments cannot substitute for evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Counsel's arguments are not evidence and cannot take the place of factual support; attorney statements about unexpected results, commercial success, etc., must be supported by affidavits/declarations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Schulze and MPEP § 2145 for case law on rebuttal arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinion evidence standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Factual evidence is preferable, but opinion testimony (expert opinion) may be considered if it is not on the ultimate legal conclusion; the examiner should weigh the basis, interest, opposing evidence, and factual support for the opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert legal conclusions are not entitled to weight, but factually supported expert opinions about factual matters (level of skill, technical observations) may be persuasive (In re Chilowsky, Lindell, Oelrich, Beattie, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight of conclusory affidavits
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits or declarations stating only conclusions may have some probative value but often little weight compared to factually-supported evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Brandstadter and other cases show conclusory statements alone are weak; provide tests/data where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant-affiant evidentiary weight
rubrics_metrics.description: An affidavit of the applicant is less persuasive than that of a disinterested person but cannot be disregarded solely because it is from the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law allows applicant affidavits some weight (Ex parte Keyes, In re McKenna) but the examiner should consider possible bias and corroborating evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighing evidence — final determination by preponderance
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate determination of patentability must be based on consideration of the entire record by a preponderance of the evidence, weighing rebuttal/secondary evidence against the prima facie case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess persuasiveness of rebuttal evidence as a whole; do not evaluate each piece only on its ability to knock down prima facie; follow In re Oetiker, Piasecki, Eli Lilly, Chupp, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain examiner's reasons when unconvinced
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner remains unconvinced after evaluating evidence, the next Office action must state that and identify the reason(s) (e.g., commercial success not convincing or not related to the technology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Demaco and follow guidance in MPEP § 2144.08 for determining sufficiency of rebuttal evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpected results — standard for difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences between claimed invention and prior art must be to such an extent that the difference is 'unexpected' — often shown by marked improvement or a difference in kind, not merely degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (Merck, Waymouth, Wagner) explains 'difference in kind' vs 'degree' and that courts scrutinize whether differences are truly unexpected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater-than-expected results evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Greater-than-expected results (including synergistic effects) can be evidence of nonobviousness, but applicants must show results exceed what would be expected from the prior art and provide significant practical advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Synergism or additive surprises may be persuasive (Corkill, Merck v. Biocraft), but such effects are not automatically sufficient — prior-art expectations must be addressed (NutraSweet example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority in a shared property as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Unexpected superiority in a property that the claimed compound shares with prior art can rebut a prima facie case of obviousness even if superiority is shown only for some applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No fixed number of examples required; see In re Chupp and Ex parte A for examples where superiority (e.g., better herbicidal control) overcame obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of an unexpected property as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstration of a property present in the claimed invention but not in the prior art (e.g., new therapeutic activity) is evidence of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Papesch and related cases show unexpected properties can be persuasive but do not automatically mandate patentability; factual support required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of an expected property as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Showing a claimed invention lacks a property that prior art would have expected it to have can be evidence of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: claimed compounds expected to have beta-blocking activity did not, which was unexpected and supported unobviousness (Ex parte Mead Johnson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on applicant to establish unexpectedness and significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants bear the burden to establish that differences in results are unexpected, unobvious, and of both statistical and practical significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere conclusions without experimental data or proper context are insufficient (Ex parte Gelles, Ex parte C); courts require statistical/practical proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicants must explain proffered data
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants bear the burden of explaining the data in any declaration proffered as evidence of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Ex parte Ishizaka; declarations should include explanation and context for tests and data presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct and indirect comparative testing probative
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct or indirect comparative tests comparing the claimed invention with the closest prior art, commensurate in scope with the claims, are probative of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Boesch, Blondel, Fouche for precedents where comparative testing was sufficient to rebut prima facie obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability of intermediates via end-product unexpectedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentability of an intermediate may be established by unexpected properties of an end product when one of ordinary skill would reasonably ascribe the intermediate as the contributing cause; applicant must identify the cause and establish a nexus between intermediate and end product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow In re Magerlein: identify contributing cause of superior end-product property and tie it factually to the claimed intermediate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighing expected versus unexpected properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Unexpected and expected properties must be weighed against each other; unexpected properties must be shown to have significance equal to or greater than expected properties to rebut obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If expected properties are more significant, unexpected properties may not be sufficient (In re Nolan, In re Eli Lilly). Expected beneficial results can be evidence of obviousness.
